facts.text: The eastern shriketit is also known as the bark tit, crested tit or yellow-bellied tit.
facts.quote: It is also known as bark tit, crested tit or yellow-bellied tit.

facts.text: The eastern shriketit has a large bill with which to lever and strip bark.
facts.quote: It has a large bill with which to lever and strip bark.

facts.text: The male eastern shriketit can raise an erectile crest, and has a black throat unlike the olive-brown throat of the female.
facts.quote: The male has an erectable crest. It has a large bill with which to lever and strip bark. The throat of the male is black, whereas that of the female is olive-brown.

facts.text: The eastern shriketit's call is a weak, mellow and mournful whistle, and it can perfectly mimic many species within its habitat.
facts.quote: The call of the eastern shriketit is a weak, mellow and mournful whistle, sounding like whiert, whit-whit, wheeir. It also makes repeated stuttering or chuckling calls described as "knock-at-the-door", and can perfectly mimic many species within its habitat.

facts.text: The eastern shriketit tears bark with its strong bill to find spiders, beetles and insect larvae, and has even been seen using a twig as a tool to poke insects out of crevices.
facts.quote: levering up and tearing bark with its strong bill to reveal prey of spiders, beetles and insect larvae. As an avian example of tool-use, it has been observed holding a twig in its bill and poking it into a crevice to obtain concealed insects.

facts.text: The eastern shriketit's nest is a deep cup of bark fibre bound with spider-web, lined with fine grass and lichen, placed up to 30 m above the ground.
facts.quote: The nest is a deep cup of bark fibre bound with spider-web, and lined with fine grass and lichen. It is usually placed among the highest twigs of a eucalypt sapling, from 5–30 m above ground where it is protected from the reach of predators.

facts.text: Clutches of 2 or 3 eggs are incubated mainly by the female for 15 or 16 days, and the young leave the nest after 14 to 17 days.
facts.quote: A clutch of 2 or 3 eggs, whitish with brown or slate-grey spots, and measuring 24 mm × 15 mm (0.9 in × 0.6 in), is incubated for 15 or 16 days mainly by the female. The young are altricial and nidicolous, fledging 14 to 17 days after hatching

facts.text: The eastern shriketit prefers the canopy of eucalypt forests and open woodlands, and is also found in trees along rivers and occasionally in rainforests.
facts.quote: Its preferred habitat is the canopy of eucalypt forests and open woodlands, and to a lesser extent stands of mallee, cypress-pine, coastal tea-tree and banksia. It is also found in trees along rivers and occasionally in rainforests.

facts.text: The eastern shriketit is endemic to Australia, ranging from tropical Queensland's Atherton Tablelands south to the Mount Lofty Ranges of South Australia.
facts.quote: The eastern shriketit is endemic to Australia. It is found in the Atherton Tablelands of tropical Queensland, southward through New South Wales and Victoria, including the Murray-Darling basin, to the Mount Lofty Ranges and Fleurieu Peninsula of South Australia.
